If you're looking at tobaccos, you're probably going to find the best selection in the FlavourArt brand, but I have a feeling you already knew I was going to promote that. I do, though, for good reason: FA's tobacco spectrum has some of the most unique, strong and combinable tobaccos I've come across yet.

You've got complex ones like Cowboy Blend and Desert Ship, you've got woodsy and oak-to-the-brim filled flavors like Shade and Dark Vapure. Lighter ones like Soho and 7 Leaves. Super high-note, spicy and peppery ones like Burley and Perique. A little of this, a little of that... I look at the FA brand of tobaccos like they're Lego blocks - unless you're just willy-nilly dumping a bunch of them on the floor and smashing them together with your foot without looking, you're probably going to get something... half-way decent.

Now, the best thing about all that is how well most of these are going to pair with things like creams, sweeteners, breads and (some) fruits. Creams and vanillas will meld flavors together nicely, using a little ethyl maltol and you're getting a smoother blend of the two. Even further when you're playing with vanilla. Unless you're trying to actually fight the profile (high, peppery notes) with creams, you're not going to come away with something too gross. At that point, it's all about adjusting to suit your tastes.

Flavorah has a couple good tobaccos as well. Cured Tobacco is fantastic at 4% straight, maybe a drop or three of EM. Mmm. MMM.

Issue I've run into a lot while trying to play with tobaccos, and I'm first and foremost a tobacco-end-of-the-spectrum kind of guy, is that a lot of them are a little too perfumey for me. A little too heavy on the floral notes (like Mild Black, I want to like it, but it always has just a twinge of something floral in there that I just can't dig). Either floral, or nuts. If I'm adding a little pecan or black walnut to a mix, I know it's in there, you know? I know where to find it if I'm looking for it. But to get a tobacco flavor chock full of nuts, like some of the old school Bakery flavors (now, easily found as Flavor Express flavorings, and there's a metric ton of tobaccos in that line) just don't touch the taste buds right for me. I'm overly picky, I know, I know.

Now, that Black Honey Tobacco and Bavarian Cream, that's a decent tasting vape - despite my dislike for bavarian cream, I can get down on that one. I have this theory. With the rise of civilization, we see the first time in human history that there existed a very marked social stratification. Hunter-gatherer tribes were pretty much extended families, so everyone had an interest in keeping the social structure relatively egalitarian. Differences in social status existed, but material wealth was distributed equally among individuals. Largely, generosity in sharing the bounties of a hunt or foraging is what determined one's social status. An exceptional hunter who didn't share was useless to the group, and thus ostracised. Envy was one mechanism by which group solidarity was secured. This is our natural way of being, and any deviation from that requires some sort of manipulation.

It is known that civilization was a result of agriculture. But, despite all the material benefits of agriculture, civilized society is unstable because it requires a class distinction between elites and laborers. Because of this inherent instability, I don't think it is a coincidence that beer was invented before bread. For such a society to survive, you need a social lubricant to make people compliant to the inherent injustice of class distinctions and a wildly exacerbated discrepancy in the distribution of material wealth.

So, to answer your question, beer.

Be content with yourself. If there is an aspect of yourself which you genuinely dislike (drug addiction, lying, depression) then work to resolve the issue at hand. Envy, like all emotions, is not inherently bad by itself. It is a perfectly normal response to stimuli, although said stimuli often varies from individual to individual. The only important thing about it is what you do about the feeling.
